newsitem.title: ALBANIA: Albania lek crumbles in dusty Tirana money market.
newsitem.headline: Albania lek crumbles in dusty Tirana money market.

text.p: The Albanian lek is taking a beating in Tirana's thriving, open-air money market as people rush to buy dollars following the dramatic disintegration of pyramid investment schemes.

With the lek down 30 percent since the start of the year, state banks have introduced tight foreign exchange curbs and even the crowds of money dealers in Tirana's unofficial street market are reluctant to sell hard currencies.
"If you think I'm going to sell dollars today you must be crazy," said Nardi, one of about 500 dealers who hawk for trade along the dusty streets outside Albania's central bank.

Inside the Bank of Albania there is stony silence over the outlook for the lek, with one official suggesting its recent freefall might be linked to general dollar strength against other European currencies.

The hordes of money dealers milling around outside disagree. "Since the collapse of the pyramids no-one wants the lek, they just want dollars," said Muli, clutching a large wad of brightly coloured lek.
"Unless the bank intervenes it will reach 150 to the dollar next week," he added. In the space of one hour, the street rate slipped to 133 from 127 and against 104 at the start of 1997.

Economists believe more than $1 billion is tied up in the pyramids saving schemes which started to fail at the end of last year, leaving many people in Europe's poorest country facing ruin and sparking social unrest.
The official bank rate was around 125 lek to the dollar on Friday but only tiny transactions were being allowed.
"There has been very little selling (of dollars) because officials are worried about panic in the monetary market," said a dealer at a state bank who declined to be named.
"There are rumours about devaluation and hyper-inflation and even some of the food shops are starting to accept just hard currencies," Muli added.

Other types of shops are happy to accept any currency, even the lek, just to keep business going. "I have only sold four pairs of shoes all week and will go bankrupt," said Arben, who owns a small shop close to the money market.

The central bank is believed to have around $270 million in foreign reserves while the street dealers say their own stash of dollars is running short, having sold over $1 million at the start of the week alone.

Their main source of hard currencies comes from Albania's army of illegal emigrants who regularly send cash back home to their families. "That money has fallen recently with many emigrants back home to try to find out what has happened to their pyramid investments," said street dealer Arist.
The only people doing roaring trade were the men selling visa application forms for the United States at 50 cents a go.

Other people came to the money changers to offer them their privatisation certificates in state companies, which Albania's right-wing government handed out last year to encourage the idea of share ownership and the free market.
The purple certificates have a face value of 40,000 lek, but pensioners trying to sell them were being offered just four percent of that.
